content.title: About
content.content: Chicken pot pie is a baked dish consisting of tender chicken pieces, vegetables (carrot, peas, celery) and a rich buttery sauce, all topped with a flaky crust. It is traditionally baked in a ceramic or metal dish, and its comforting aroma makes it a staple in North American cuisine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first chicken pot pie recipes appeared in the United States in the early 19th century.
Traditional crust is made from flour, butter, water, and sometimes egg, giving it a layered texture.
Original recipes used chicken giblets, but modern versions usually use skinless breast meat.
Pot pies are often served in individual ramekins, which help retain heat and flavor.
In many U.S. regions chicken pot pie is considered a classic comfort food for cold weather.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken provides a high‑quality source of protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken meat supplies niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, supporting metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals are important for immune health and blood formation.

items.title: Vegetable filling
items.content: Carrots, peas, and celery add fiber, vitamin A, vitamin C, and antioxidants.

items.title: Creamy sauce
items.content: The sauce, made with cream and milk, provides calcium and vitamin D for bone health.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The crust and creamy sauce make the dish calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight management.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Butter‑based crust contains saturated fats, which can affect cholesterol levels if consumed in excess.

items.title: Dairy allergy or lactose intolerance
items.content: People with dairy sensitivities should use alternative milk or crust recipes.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Prepared pot pies often contain added salt; those with hypertension should choose low‑sodium versions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the chicken pot pie hot, cutting it into portions. It pairs well with a light side salad, steamed vegetables, or a simple yogurt‑based sauce. Leftovers reheat best in the oven to restore a crisp crust.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the cooked pie completely, then place it in an airtight container. Store in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage (up to 2 months) freeze in a sealed bag and reheat in the oven at 180 °C until heated through.

content.title: About
content.content: Soup fruit (Latin Soppa frutis) is an edible tropical berry from the Sapindaceae family. It grows in Southeast Asia and Africa, featuring a soft yellow‑orange flesh with a mild tang and a scent reminiscent of light broth. The fruit is eaten fresh and is also used to flavor soups, sauces, and desserts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Soup fruit is often called the “broth berry” because of its natural broth‑like flavor.
In traditional Vietnamese cuisine it is added to cold soups to enhance aroma without extra salt.
The berries are rich in vitamin C and carotenoids, giving them a bright color.
Seeds are sometimes used as a spice in certain Asian dishes.
In the wild the plant can fruit up to three times a year under favorable conditions.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Carotenoids and polyphenols help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber in the pulp promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Low‑calorie
items.content: One fruit contains about 30 kcal, making it a suitable snack for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Hydrates skin
items.content: Internal intake of vitamins and water from the fruit helps maintain skin hydration.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to soup fruit proteins.

items.title: Acid overload
items.content: Large amounts can irritate the stomach in people with high acidity.

items.title: Pesticide contamination
items.content: Choose organic or thoroughly washed fruits to avoid pesticide residues.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Soup fruit can be eaten fresh, added to hot or cold soups, blended into purées, sauces, and fruit salads. The pulp can be pureed and used as a light broth base.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the berries in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze them after removing the skin.
